extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; historians of American media; journalism professionals interested in late-19th/early-20th century press
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting standards and evaluative criteria used in assessing/producing American newspapers circa 1892–1914 (layout, business model, editorial practice, circulation, chains, and technological/typographic choices). Useful for analyzing period journalism or comparing historical newsroom practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of banner lines / huge display heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Banner line—for major news-breaks, at least—had come to stay; hand-drawn block type several inches high was used (e.g., New York Evening Journal), and some papers ran streamer lines of heavy block type often two or three inches high during the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Journal’s hand-drawn elephant-sized heads, Chicago Tribune triple banner in heavy Gothic for Dewey’s victory, Pittsburgh Commercial Gazette streamer lines. Note: extremely large display type sometimes required special production techniques (hand-drawn, crude cuts) because metal type of such sizes was not readily procurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline color and red banners
rubrics_metrics.description: Streamers or banner lines were sometimes printed in red; the Denver Post began its red banners in 1899.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color (red) used as emphasis on front-page banners; became a device associated with sensational or major-news presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page make-up consistency vs lawless variety
rubrics_metrics.description: There was so much lawless variety in front-page make-up that it amounted to monstrous confusion; some papers kept modest single-column heads and refused to break column rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied criterion: avoid 'lawless' or incoherent front-page layouts — strive for balance between attention-getting banners and readable, orderly layout. The New York Times later showed that conservatism in make-up can convey dependability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting column rules vs breaking them for display
rubrics_metrics.description: While many papers used double- and triple-column heads for big stories, not a few refused to break column rules at all and appeared with modest single-column heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial/layout choice: decide whether to prioritize dramatic display (full-width banners) or strict columnar order (single-column heads) depending on editorial identity and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic/production limits of display type
rubrics_metrics.description: Wood-type did not work well in forms, and metal type of such sizes could not be procured; 'The largest size in favor ... made it impossible to use more than five letters in the width of a newspaper page.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production constraint: size of headlines constrained by available type and printing technology; must balance desired visual impact with technical feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale: circulation, pages, advertising volume, staff size
rubrics_metrics.description: Big newspapers grew in circulations, number of pages per issue, and volume of advertising; e.g., New York World had annual expenses of about $2,000,000 and a full-time force of 1,300; regular daily editions of 16–24 pages and Sunday 48–72 with nearly half advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these quantitative measures (circulation numbers, page counts, advertising percentage, staff size, expense/revenue figures) to gauge a paper's scale and commercial importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial conservatism / business stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Big business in newspapers tended to buttress and steady the structure with financial conservatism; 'Journalistic success brings money. The editor has become a money man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: financial stability and conservative business practices are indicators of a mature newspaper capable of long-term investment and resisting fickle trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of editorial and business influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-established journals were in a better position to resent undue interference with proper journalistic functions; Ochs could defy even an angry advertiser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial independence from advertisers and owners is a marker of journalistic integrity and credibility; evaluate whether editorial policy yields to advertising pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and dependability of news service
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times' exchange of special news services with the London Times helped bring foreign coverage to a high level of excellence; dependable financial news and full, trustworthy coverage of governmental and political news (with texts of speeches and documents) made the paper indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess newspapers on the thoroughness, trustworthiness, and international reach of their news-gathering and reporting services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative, dependable make-up and editorial tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Conservatism in headlines and make-up, avoiding flashiness on the one hand and complete monotony on the other, combined with good printing and careful editing, gave an impression of dependability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and tone should aim for credibility: not flashy sensationalism, but also not dull monotony. Balance helps build trust with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing strategy as circulation/business lever
rubrics_metrics.description: The Times cut its price per copy from three cents to a penny to challenge the yellow papers and rapidly increased circulation and advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use price-per-copy and promotional pricing strategically to alter circulation dynamics; this is a business metric affecting readership and revenue mix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content diversification and supplements
rubrics_metrics.description: Additions such as an excellent Sunday supplement with halftones on book-paper, a Saturday book review section, and a Monday financial review were used to improve a paper and attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering specialized sections and high-quality supplements can enhance a paper's appeal and readership demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain-building and low-cost founding model (Scripps method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripps' method: found new papers rather than buy established ones; choose a city (50,000–100,000), advance about $25,000, pick a manager, pay $25/week until money runs out, and give stock to the manager if profitable; Scripps took the loss if paper failed and 51% if it succeeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for expansion strategy: low-capital, manager-incentivized model aimed at mass-market afternoon papers in small-to-medium cities; success measured by profitability and ability to scale to a chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeting the masses and editorial advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripps properties were cheap afternoon papers published for the masses; Scripps: 'I have constituted myself the advocate of that large majority of people who are not so rich ...' — crusaders against utility abuses and political bossism, aligned with labor and liberalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial positioning—advocacy for working/middle classes—serves as a defining criterion for a paper's identity and local influence; impacts audience and editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to advertiser control / editorial integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripps insisted that editorial policy should never yield an inch to even the heaviest department-store patronage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a paper's commitment to editorial independence by its willingness to resist advertiser pressure even at financial cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with adless formats and tabloid forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripps financed experimental adless tabloids (Chicago Day Book) and the Philadelphia News-Post (adless), attempting novel formats to reach readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovative formats (adless, tabloid narrow columns, heavy picture content) can be evaluated by their circulation performance and financial sustainability; experiments show appetite for nontraditional business models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managerial competence and business acumen
rubrics_metrics.description: Munsey's trial-and-error approach, meddling, and managerial failures illustrate that managerial competence (or lack thereof) is central: Munsey was often a failure as a newspaper manager despite journalistic ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proprietors and managers on ability to run papers profitably, preserve readership, and implement sustainable editorial/business strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of printing technology and visual quality (halftones, color presses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investments in halftones on book-paper, color presses, and good printing were cited as ways to improve the paper’s appearance and attract readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printing quality and photographic/typographic capabilities are evaluative metrics for production value and perceived modernity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political alignment and influence in local contests
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers' political stances (e.g., Sun breaking with the Gorman machine; Evening News crusading against patronage) affected elections and local politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newspapers by their political alignment and the effectiveness of their advocacy in shaping local/national political outcomes.
